intro: Compare cc vs mL with zero math guesswork: 1 cubic centimeter (1 cc or 1 cm³) equals exactly 1 milliliter (1 mL), so the conversion ratio is always 1:1. Clinicians, pharmacists, mechanics, and lab technicians often see both labels on syringes, liquid medications, and engine specs, even though modern medical safety standards prefer mL to avoid misreading 'cc' as 'u' (units). Look up dosages from 0.1 cm³ to 1,000 cm³ below.

mistakesAndEdgeCases.title: Why Hospitals Prefer 'mL' Over 'cc' & Drop Volume Variation
items: Although 1 cc and 1 mL are identical in volume, The Joint Commission and ISMP place 'cc' on the medical Do Not Use abbreviation list because handwritten 'cc' can be misread as 'u' (units) or '00'—always chart medication doses in mL.

A liquid 'drop' (gtt) is not a standardized SI unit: standard metric medicine droppers dispense roughly 0.05 cc (20 drops per mL), whereas IV micro-drip tubing dispenses 60 drops per mL (0.0167 cc/drop). Always measure critical doses with a graduated syringe.

faqs.question: Are cc and mL the same?
faqs.answer: Yes. One cubic centimeter (1 cc or 1 cm³) equals exactly 1 milliliter (1 mL) by SI definition. Any measurement in cc has the exact same numerical value in mL.

faqs.question: How many cc are in a drop?
faqs.answer: A standard metric medical drop is about 0.05 cc (0.05 mL), meaning roughly 20 drops equal 1 cc (1 mL). Drop volume depends on liquid viscosity and tip diameter—for instance, IV micro-drip sets deliver 60 drops per cc (0.0167 cc per drop).

faqs.question: How many mL is 6 cc?
faqs.answer: 6 cc equals exactly 6 mL (slightly more than 1 US teaspoon, which is 4.93 mL).

faqs.question: Is a cubic centimeter the same as a milliliter for both liquids and engines?
faqs.answer: Yes, both represent a 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm cube (1/1,000 of a liter). By convention, mL is standard for medications and liquids, while cc or cm³ is commonly used for engine displacement and solid volumes.
